newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela hits back at de Klerk racism claims.
newsitem.headline: Mandela hits back at de Klerk racism claims.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela hit back on Wednesday at claims by his predecessor F.W. de Klerk that his party used racism as a political tool.

"I challenge any one of you who were in government and left -- (you) don't have the record we in the ANC...have established in accommodating all racial groups in this country," he said in a speech to parliament.
De Klerk, in a speech on Tuesday responding to Mandela's state of the nation address at Friday's opening of parliament, accused the ruling party of playing the racist card.

"The African National Congress, despite its lip service to non-racialism and reconciliation, plays a hard game of racist politics and incites racist emotions whenever it suits itself," he said, exactly seven years after he freed Mandela from jail.
"I want to accuse the ANC today...that it is plunging the country into a form of new apartheid and that it is fomenting colour prejudices."

Mandela, whose own commitment to reconciliation among his country's long-divided races has stayed beyond question in party political slanging matches, stood up for his policy of affirmative action for people who were oppressed by apartheid.
"This whole hue and cry about affirmative action being a reverse form of racism is a misplaced perception," he said, deviating from his prepared speech to answer racism charges.

Many whites but especially Afrikaners, who had sheltered employment in state jobs under apartheid, claim they are now being victimised and face bleak career prospects in the new "rainbow" South Africa.
De Klerk's National Party introduced apartheid in 1948 and began dismantling it in 1990, which led to all-race elections for the first time in 1994.
The now reformed party is still dominated by whites and is facing an uphill battle in its struggle to win the votes of blacks who make up 80 percent of the population.

Mandela, who served 27 years in jail for treason against the apartheid state, said on Wednesday he had been encouraged by the response from business and workers to the government's 1997 plan of action he outlined in his Friday address.
"The message we are getting is that the country is on the right track; there is cause to be optimistic about the future," he said.
"We are one people with one destiny."
